newsitem.title: FRANCE: France welcomes EU farm set-aside "deal".
newsitem.headline: France welcomes EU farm set-aside "deal".

text.p: France's farm ministry on Wednesday welcomed what it said was a deal to keep the European Union's set-aside unchanged at five percent next year, saying it would bolster France's position on the world grain market.
EU farm ministers in Luxembourg earlier called for an unchanged rate of five percent of cereals set-aside as part of a marathon price package hammered out over nearly three days.

But the European Commission, which must first formally propose a set-aside rate before one can be agreed, said it was not bound by the ministers' decision. It vowed not to be bounced into making a hasty proposal until it had data on the next crop.

"The aim was to keep set-aside as low as possible," the farm ministry in Paris said in a statement. "It is set at five percent, which corresponds to the market and reinforces Europe's potential to be present on the world grain market."

Set-aside is an EU scheme meant to contain grain surpluses by deliberately leaving some land fallow. The set-aside rate is the proportion of their land grain farmers must leave idle in order to qualify for EU subsidies. The rate has been gradually reduced from 15 percent over several years.

European Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler said in Luxembourg the EU executive would make a proposal on the set-aside rate for 1998 as soon as possible and was not bound by the farm ministers' decision to leave it unchanged at five percent.
"The Commission is free to make a proposal and that's what we'll do as soon as possible," Fischler told journalists after the ministers had agreed next year's farm price package.
In a statement issued after the end of the three-day talks, the Commission said Fischler respected the Council's right to suggest a set-aside rate.

But he added, "this is a market management instrument and the rate should be established in an objective way on the basis of the most up to date information on the market outlook. This will be basis upon which the Commssion will draw up its proposal on set-aside."
French officials and industry groups had before the meeting made plain their preference to have set-aside brought to zero, while Germany had pushed for a larger rate of 10 percent.
French farm groups welcomed the five percent set-aside recommendation by EU ministers as a "reasonable compromise."
The powerful FNSEA farm union said it went in the direction of France's ultimate goal of abolishing set-aside altogether.
The AGPB French wheat producers' association said the decision was reasonable but the low level of stocks would have justified getting rid of the unpopular idling scheme entirely.
The French Chambers of Agricultural Commerce said set-aside was "usless and discriminatory" and should be ditched. But the decision to leave it where it was showed "good sense" for now.
Farm analysts say bringing set-aside to zero would in fact make little difference to the amount of grain produced because farmers have left only their least fertile land in the scheme.
